Accenture Earnings: Five Straight Beats Set a High Bar for October 1
As seen on the 24/7 Wall St. homepage on October 1, 2026.
Accenture reports before the open with five straight EPS beats behind it, so consensus of $3.18 is the low bar. The real tell is whether AI consulting demand is still offsetting cautious enterprise IT budgets.
Accenture reports fiscal fourth-quarter results before the opening bell on October 1, and five consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street's earnings-per-share estimate mean the market will treat anything merely in line with the $3.18 consensus as a disappointment.
The more consequential question sitting underneath that number is what management says about AI-driven consulting demand. Investors have been watching whether that business is strong enough to absorb the drag from corporations still guarding their broader IT budgets carefully, and the language in the outlook will carry as much weight as the headline figure.
Accenture is large enough that its commentary effectively serves as a read on enterprise technology spending across the global economy. A confident tone on forward bookings would reinforce the bull case; anything cautious would ripple through the IT services sector well beyond this single report.
Because the release lands before the open, any gap in the stock at the start of trading will reflect the market's instant verdict on both the number and the guidance. Investors who want to understand where enterprise tech sentiment stands will have their answer within the first hour of the session.

Accenture opened 22% higher, a move you almost never see from a mega-cap IT services name, while Corteva dropped 82% to $13.96 at the other end of the board. Synopsys, McKesson and IBM round out a gainers list that is all up at least 5.9%.
Accenture topped both lines again and set FY27 EPS guidance at $14.39 to $14.81, the clearest read yet that enterprise AI budgets are still landing in consultants' pockets.

Accenture Federal Services and Google Public Sector Establish Gemini Launchpads to Power Purpose-Built Agents Across Federal Missions
Accenture Federal Services and Google Public Sector Establish Gemini Launchpads to Power Purpose-Built Agents Across Federal Missions · Business Wire
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 6:47 AM CDT 5 min read
WASHINGTON, October 19, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Accenture Federal Services, a subsidiary of Accenture (NYSE: ACN), and Google Public Sector today announced the deployment of Gemini launchpads, a new capability designed to help federal agencies move more quickly from agentic experimentation to mission execution at scale.
This initiative, which builds on the recent announcement of Accenture's Gemini Enterprise Business Group (part of the Accenture Google Business Group), provides federal agencies with a centralized hub of Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs) to industrialize how they build, deploy, and scale enterprise agents. By embedding these specialized FDEs alongside agencies, the government can focus on delivering outcome-based, high-code agents built on Gemini, that integrate directly into core government systems of record and enable practitioners to execute complex workflows.
By activating a Gemini launchpad, agencies can centrally manage the agent–from securely connecting Gemini to mission datasets and prioritizing agent use cases to rapid deployment and workforce training. This provides leadership with a single view to track performance, measure mission impact, and drive even more value from their investment in Gemini.
"The real opportunity to scale value for our clients is deploying these purpose-built agents to transform work at the heart of government operations," said Ron Ash, CEO of Accenture Federal Services. "By embedding our Forward Deployed Engineers with agency teams, we're working side-by-side with our clients to help them define and rapidly solve their most critical challenges using agents to help deliver the advantage our clients need and the results they expect."
"Federal agencies stand at the threshold of the agentic era, where success is measured not merely by technology adopted, but by mission outcomes delivered," said Karen Dahut, CEO of Google Public Sector. "By pairing Gemini and secure cloud infrastructure with Accenture Federal Services' deep federal acumen, we are enabling agencies to build purpose-driven agents designed for the way they work. This collaboration further moves governments beyond incremental modernization—equipping public servants with intelligent capabilities to navigate complex systems, accelerate critical decisions, and deliver at the speed of mission."
Accelerating Mission Impact with Specialized Engineers and Pre-Built Agents
To meet federal demand and accelerate this mission, Accenture Federal Services is training an initial cohort of Google Cloud- skilled FDEs. This training would be part of Accenture's recently announced commitment to establish a 1,000-person FDE workforce Accenture Gemini Enterprise Business Group.
These FDEs will embed directly alongside agency teams and Accenture Federal's functional subject matter experts to bridge the gap between technology and mission. By combining advanced Google Cloud technical skills with deep federal domain expertise, these integrated teams will build Gemini agents that address real agency challenges and unlock tangible mission value.
To jumpstart agency adoption, Accenture Federal Services and Google Public Sector are developing a core set of pre-built agents across common mission-critical functions including HR, finance, and supply chain. These agents are purpose-built to streamline daily operations directly within Gemini. By handling complex workflows and data-gathering behind the scenes, these agents free federal employees to focus on decision-making and strategic mission execution.
"Executing this vision requires a combination of the right technology and mission experience," said Garrett Berntsen, Chief AI Officer, Accenture Federal Services. "Google Public Sector provides the industry-leading infrastructure and frontier models, while Accenture Federal brings the deep domain expertise and engineering talent needed to solve complex mission challenges. Together, we are putting Google's integrated tech stack to work to drive measurable outcomes for our customers."
Federal agencies can see these capabilities in action by engaging in collaborative, hands-on agent building workshops hosted jointly with Google Public Sector at The Forge in Washington, D.C. Recently launched within The Forge, The Prototyping Lab is a dedicated agentic prototyping space designed specifically to walk agency leaders through diverse, live agent experiences across various business and mission functions. During these interactive sessions, Accenture and Google Public Sector collaborate directly to identify the highest-impact agents for specific outcomes and outline a tactical roadmap to get started.
Accenture Federal Services is a US subsidiary of Accenture LLP that government agencies choose to drive impactful change. Our 15,000 people are committed to powering reinvention for the federal government with the same commercial technology, competitive drive and technical edge that is transforming global industry—ensuring that federal enterprises can be as modern, fast, and efficient as the country it serves. See how we reinvent at www.accenturefederal.com.
Accenture helps the world's leading enterprises reinvent by building their digital core and unleashing the power of AI to create value at speed for organizations across industries. Our strategy is to be the reinvention partner of choice for our clients and lead in the safe, widespread adoption of AI, and to be the most client-focused, AI-enabled, great place to work in the world. We bring together the talent of our approximately 814,000 people with proprietary assets and platforms, deep process and industry expertise, and leading ecosystem relationships to deliver end-to-end solutions and measurable outcomes at scale. Through our Reinvention Services, we offer broad expertise across Cybersecurity, Digital Core, Finance, Industry and Enterprise, Song, Supply Chain and Engineering, and Talent, with advanced capabilities in AI and Data, Industry and Process, and Technology. We serve approximately 9,000 clients and generated approximately $74 billion in FY26 revenue. Visit us at accenture.com.

bear_case: Accenture's discretionary spending remains vulnerable to economic uncertainty and pricing competition. AI-driven efficiencies are reshaping delivery models and workforce needs, potentially leading to cost pressures. Elevated acquisition spending and financing costs add execution risk, while federal contracting remains sensitive to policy changes despite a recent recovery. Investor concerns that AI could lead clients to bring work in-house could impact Accenture's service delivery model. A China sale could help fund Accenture's $8bn in planned acquisitions for fiscal 2027, but the transaction's timing and execution are uncertain. Tighter Chinese security rules limiting sensitive data export could impact Accenture's operations in the Greater China business. Compliance wrapper for Gemini for Government Services is being sold, potentially introducing regulatory risks. Corporate insider sentiment is negative on the stock. First-quarter revenue landing below $18.95 billion may challenge the AI cost discipline policy. If AI tool costs pressure margins, Accenture's fiscal 2027 EPS guidance could be impacted.

Accenture, Dragos and SANS Institute Launch Foundation to Strengthen Cyber Defenses for Under-Resourced U.S. Utilities Accenture, Dragos Inc. and the SANS Institute today announced a major initiative to help strengthen cyber defenses for under-resourced U.S. water, electric and natural gas utilities. Tue, October 20, 2026 at 12:59 PM CDT 7 min read Approximately $10 million in initial funding and services will support essential services relied on by more than 100 million Americans Initiative will provide technology, deployment services and training at no cost to up to 500 under-resourced utilities COLUMBUS, Ohio, October 20, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Accenture (NYSE: ACN), Dragos Inc. and the SANS Institute today announced a major initiative to help strengthen cyber defenses for under-resourced U.S. water, electric and natural gas utilities. These utilities provide essential services but often lack resources for adequate protection for their operational technology (OT) environments. The announcement comes amid a recent surge in cyberattacks targeting more than 100 U.S. water systems across over a dozen states. In its first phase, the initiative will provide cybersecurity software, hardware, deployment services and SANS training free of charge to up to 500 under-resourced utilities. Accenture, Dragos and SANS are making an initial combined commitment of approximately $10 million in funding and services. In addition, Elastic is supporting the initiative through technology that allows for software delivery at scale by providing the primary log storage and query engine within the Dragos Platform. Many of the tens of thousands of small utilities across the U.S., particularly those serving rural or underserved communities, face limited funding, workforce shortages and aging technology. This leaves the pumps, valves, substations and distribution networks that support essential services vulnerable to cyberattacks that can threaten public safety. To address this gap, Accenture, Dragos and SANS are launching the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation to provide eligible utilities with OT cybersecurity technology, deployment support, hardware and training. The initiative builds on the Dragos Community Defense Program, which provides more than 100 utilities with free access to the Dragos Platform. The foundation was announced at a roundtable discussion focused on strengthening the cybersecurity of utilities in Ohio, hosted by American Electric Power (AEP) subsidiary Ohio Power Company, Accenture and Dragos. Bernstein just reversed its Datadog call one quarter after a downgrade shook the stock, pointing to AI token consumption as the reason. Whether that optimism survives the November earnings report is the question every investor in the space should be…
Published October 19, 2026, 10:47am ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Amidst glowing server racks, a technician manages the critical AI infrastructure that underpins the 'neocloud' services discussed in the article, highlighting the intense competition between companies like CoreWeave and Nebius. © baranozdemir / Getty Images
Signs of accelerating AI workloads are pulling cloud software back into favor after a rough stretch for technology names. Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG | DDOG Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $259.15 in morning trading, leading the group higher.
Bernstein upgraded Datadog stock to Outperform from Market Perform, stating that its data show enterprise AI token consumption at the largest AI labs growing rapidly quarter over quarter. The new rating rests on the conclusion that the earlier view of Datadog’s AI-driven growth was too conservative, a reversal that comes one quarter after a downgrade tied to a revenue cut at Datadog’s largest AI-native customer and slower demand among established clients.
A broad selloff in technology stocks the prior week sets the background for the upgrade. Observability software from Datadog tracks how applications and cloud infrastructure perform, so more AI tokens moving through customer systems could translate into more activity for the company to monitor and bill.
Second-quarter 2026 results already gave Datadog’s AI story a solid base. The company posted revenue of $1.12 billion, up 35.6% from a year earlier, and non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) of $0.65, beating expectations. That marked Datadog’s fifth consecutive EPS beat.
Datadog’s larger accounts kept expanding as well, with customers paying $100,000 or more in annual recurring revenue up 23% to approximately 4,720. Growth in that tier picked up from 21% in the first quarter of 2026.
Management raised Datadog’s full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $4.45 billion and $4.47 billion after that report. Chief executive Olivier Pomel tied the momentum to AI. He made the point in the August release, stating, “Our customers are building and deploying with AI, and they are using the Datadog platform to observe, secure, and act on their AI-enabled solutions.”
Datadog has been shipping products aimed directly at AI customers, including Bits AI for autonomous incident detection and resolution, AI Guard for protecting AI agents, and Bits Agent Builder for creating custom agents. The company launched more than 100 new capabilities at its DASH 2026 conference, including a Bring Your Own Cloud model that runs Datadog inside customer environments. It also acquired Adaptive ML to speed up its AI research.
That product push came alongside better profitability, with Datadog’s non-GAAP operating margin expanding to 23% from 20% a year earlier. Its free cash flow margin reached 25% in the quarter.
Snowflake and Cloudflare Trail the Leader
Checking in on the peers, Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) stock is up 3%, a solid gain that still trails the jump in Datadog stock. Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is up 0.4% to $297.58, lagging both Datadog stock and Snowflake stock. Snowflake sells a cloud data platform, while Cloudflare runs a network for security and content delivery.
Sector-wide gains are more modest, as the WisdomTree Cloud Computing Fund (NASDAQ:WCLD) is up 0.8%. Broader tech is running ahead of cloud software, as the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is up 1%. That gap leaves the jump in Datadog stock looking like a company-specific reaction to the upgrade.
Bernstein Upgrade Sets Up Datadog’s November Report
Datadog is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 results in early November, with its guidance calling for revenue of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion. Datadog’s report needs to show AI-native customers spending more, since the upgrade rests on AI workload growth. Another focus is whether established customers also step up their spending after the slower demand behind last quarter’s downgrade.
Last quarter’s downgrade is a reminder that Datadog’s growth depends partly on its largest AI-native customer. When all is said and done, investors should keep their Datadog stock positions moderate. A second revenue cut could undo the optimism behind the new rating, and the prior week’s tech selloff showed how quickly sentiment can turn.

Cloud software stocks are under heavy pressure as worries about AI financing spread across the sector. High-growth names that posted strong recent results are absorbing much of the selling.
Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW | SNOW Price Prediction) stock is down 7% at $310.83 early in the session, leading the cloud group lower. Likewise, Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is down 7% to $293.45. Meanwhile, Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) stock is down 6% to $249.08, representing a slightly smaller decline than its peers.
Sector funds are falling far less. The First Trust Cloud Computing ETF (NASDAQ:SKYY) is down 4%, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 1.35%. In other words, large-cap tech is slipping but cloud-computing stocks are generally declining faster.
AI Financing Fears Hit High-Growth Cloud Names
This decline extends a rotation out of AI-linked stocks as investors question how AI infrastructure spending gets financed. Snowflake added its own wrinkle in late September, when it proposed a convertible note offering. Those notes can later convert into equity, placing Snowflake directly inside the financing debate.
Each company sells a different piece of the cloud: Snowflake offers a data platform, Cloudflare runs a global network for security and content delivery, and Datadog sells software that tracks applications and infrastructure. That mix ties revenue at all three to cloud usage, so an AI spending pullback could hit them at once (we featured seven suppliers supporting the AI expansion, from power to networking, in a free report you can grab here).
Strong Earnings Haven’t Shielded Snowflake
Snowflake’s latest results were strong. In its Q2 FY2027 report on September 2, Snowflake posted revenue of $1.55 billion, up 35.1% year over year, along with non-GAAP EPS of $0.62 that beat estimates.
Management also raised Snowflake’s fiscal 2027 product revenue guidance to $6.07 billion from $5.84 billion. Its net revenue retention held at 126%, and remaining performance obligations reached $9 billion. Those figures suggest customers are expanding their commitments to the platform.
AI adoption is adding to Snowflake’s momentum. CoCo passed 9,100 accounts in the quarter, while CoWork expanded to 5,800 accounts. Executives called AI a “powerful flywheel” for consumption.
One concern surfaced on Snowflake’s September earnings call. The company cut its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP product gross margin guidance to 74% because fast-growing AI workloads carry a lower contribution margin. Then-CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy stated “As models have gotten more powerful, cost has absolutely become a concern.”
Cloudflare Steers Clear of the AI Capex Race
Cloudflare has taken a more selective path on AI spending, even as it restructures around what it calls an “agentic AI-first operating model.” On its Q2 2026 earnings call in August, then-CEO Matthew Prince explained why Cloudflare avoids selling commodity compute:
I think not all revenue is created equal. And if you’re selling what is just commodity compute, if you’re basically letting, you know, an AI company use your balance sheet and your credit rating in order to buy servers that are the same as everybody else’s servers, that’s just not attractive business for us.
Prince added that Cloudflare has “always focused on how we can squeeze as much out of every CapEx dollar as possible.” That sets Cloudflare apart from hyperscalers that buy servers and lease them back.
Yet, that discipline hasn’t insulated Cloudflare stock. Datadog has leaned into AI with launches such as Bits AI and AI Guard, and Datadog shares are doing slightly better, though still trailing the cloud ETF.
Snowflake’s Financing Question Hangs Over Cloud Names
Snowflake’s bull case rests on demand for data platforms that feed AI workloads, backed by three straight quarters of accelerating product revenue growth. Cloudflare bulls point to its capital discipline, and Datadog bulls to AI monitoring demand. The bear case for all three: investors keep marking down AI-linked names until financing concerns ease.
The next test for Snowflake is whether AI demand keeps product revenue growth on its guided path. Traders may want to check for whether SKYY closes its gap with QQQ.
Strong recent results give Snowflake, Cloudflare, and Datadog a fundamental buffer, while the financing concern could keep the three stocks volatile. Position sizes should be kept small, if you choose to invest at all, until the AI financing question resolves.

Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

Datadog Reports Q3 on November 4 After Bernstein's Upgrade. Here's the Number That Settles the In-House Debate ©@iJeab via Canva, @kasto via Canva
What Happened?
Datadog (DDOG) closed at $260.36 on October 19, 2026, up 5.36%, after Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform and raised its target to $350 from $237. That target sits above the $340 high in TIKR's October 16 Street data. Shares remain 11.22% below their October 9 closing high of $293.26.
Bernstein's analyst also flagged that customers who get big enough have tended to bring monitoring in-house. Datadog's CFO made a different case a month earlier, and pointed to a runway the upgrade does not address. Third-quarter results arrive before the market opens on November 4, per Datadog's investor relations materials.
Datadog's CFO Says the Cloud Shift Is Still Early
At Goldman Sachs' Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 10, CFO David Obstler pointed to how little of the market has moved. "The research companies say that somewhere upper 20s, 30% of applications are in the cloud," he said. He added that many enterprises "really haven't even started their first material projects." He cited Datadog's customer announcements in banking, insurance, automotive, manufacturing, and airlines as evidence that migration is under way.
To catch those projects, salespeople in Datadog's key accounts group now cover one or two accounts "where the IT budget and conversion to the cloud can be in the tens of millions." On the in-house question, Obstler described AI-native customers moving the other way: "we're seeing a movement from open source or initial efforts or cobbling it together towards Datadog."
Customers with $100,000 or more in annual recurring revenue reached about 4,720 at the end of the second quarter, up 23% from a year earlier. Obstler called these enterprise sales cycles very long, so that count tracks the strategy better than any single quarter's revenue.
Datadog Trades at Twice the Peer Median on Revenue
At the October 16 close, Datadog's enterprise value traded at around 17 times NTM revenue. The median for the nine companies in TIKR's software comparison set, which runs from Microsoft (MSFT) to RingCentral (RNG), was around 8 times. The October 19 gain pushed Datadog's multiple higher.
Margins support part of that premium. Datadog's second-quarter adjusted EBIT margin widened 307 basis points year over year to 22.92%, while revenue grew 35.64%.
The known gap is the largest customer. Datadog said in August that the account had renewed but that its usage would decline starting in the third quarter, a cut built into guidance. Obstler did not claim every customer stays fully on the platform: "it isn't the case all the time, and it also isn't 100% or 0%." Before Bernstein's upgrade, TIKR's October 16 data showed a mean target of around $290, with 33 Buys, 10 Outperforms, 3 Holds, 1 Underperform, and 1 Sell.
The TIKR model's mid case values Datadog at around $726 by December 31, 2030, a total return of around 179% from $260.36, or around 28% a year over 4.2 years. It is a scenario built on assumptions, not a forecast.
Over the model's 2025 to 2035 forecast, the mid case assumes around 21% annual revenue growth and a net income margin near 29%, against 24.4% over the past year on the model card. The primary risk is a valuation reset toward the peer median before those margins arrive.
On the upside, adjusted margins are already widening. On the downside, a multiple at the peer median of around 8 times revenue would be less than half of Datadog's October 16 level.
November 4 shows whether AI-native customers keep moving onto Datadog, as Obstler described, or in-house, as Bernstein warned. Growth in $100,000-plus customers at or above the second quarter's 23% pace would support the premium. A slowdown below 20% would make the gap to the peer median harder to defend.

Datadog shares rose 6% today after Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform and raised its price target to $350 from $237.
Bernstein's case for faster AI-driven growth looks well-founded, but the stock already prices in a lot of it.
Analysts expect revenue to grow about 30% this year, then slow to about 23% a year through 2028.
Third-quarter results on Nov. 4 are the first real test of whether AI-native customers can make up for slower traditional customers.
Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) shares are up 6% today. Before the open, Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform from Market Perform and raised its price target to $350 from $237.
The bounce follows a drop of about 14% last week in a broad tech selloff.
It's quite the reversal. Bernstein downgraded Datadog last quarter for two reasons. Its largest "Born in AI" customer (widely reported to be OpenAI) cut about $100 million of annual recurring revenue. And demand looked softer among the traditional customers that make up around 85% of revenue. At the time, Bernstein expected growth from AI-native customers to slow to 50%-60% in 2027, from 80%-90% this year.
Now Bernstein analyst Peter Weed says that view was too conservative:
"Our alt data signals suggest enterprise token consumption appears to have grown at least 50% [quarter over quarter] among the largest AI Labs (and perhaps even faster in their smaller 'Born in AI' customers)."
He added that consumer AI agents like Muse and Dots could raise the monitoring needs of Datadog's traditional customers too.
Wall Street's estimates already have Datadog growing fast for years…

Consensus has revenue climbing about 30% this year to $4.47 billion, then slowing to about 23% a year, reaching $6.78 billion in 2028. Bernstein is betting against that slowdown. If the biggest AI labs keep adding usage at anything like 50% a quarter, those later years look conservative to me.
Of course, more tokens don't turn straight into Datadog revenue. And Weed himself points out that customers who get big enough have tended to move monitoring in-house.
Shares were up about 82% this year through Friday's close, and the valuation has followed…
Datadog (DDOG): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)
At Friday's close, Datadog traded at 93.2x forward earnings, and after today's jump it's closer to 99x. That's under its five-year average of 107.6x, which the 2021 bubble pushed up. But it's about double the 47.4x the stock hit in February.
My take: Bernstein's upgrade looks well-founded. If AI-native customers keep growing like this, Datadog's revenue should beat what the Street expects for 2027 and 2028.
But at nearly 100x forward earnings, the stock needs proof. Datadog reports third-quarter results on Nov. 4. That will be the first real look at whether its AI-native customers are making up for any slowdown among its traditional ones.

Datadog Jumps 5% as Bernstein Upgrade Cites AI Demand; Snowflake Rises 3%, Cloudflare Holds Steady
Bernstein just reversed its Datadog call one quarter after a downgrade shook the stock, pointing to AI token consumption as the reason. Whether that optimism survives the November earnings report is the question every investor in the space should be…
Published October 19, 2026, 10:47am ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Amidst glowing server racks, a technician manages the critical AI infrastructure that underpins the 'neocloud' services discussed in the article, highlighting the intense competition between companies like CoreWeave and Nebius. © baranozdemir / Getty Images
Signs of accelerating AI workloads are pulling cloud software back into favor after a rough stretch for technology names. Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG | DDOG Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $259.15 in morning trading, leading the group higher.
Bernstein upgraded Datadog stock to Outperform from Market Perform, stating that its data show enterprise AI token consumption at the largest AI labs growing rapidly quarter over quarter. The new rating rests on the conclusion that the earlier view of Datadog’s AI-driven growth was too conservative, a reversal that comes one quarter after a downgrade tied to a revenue cut at Datadog’s largest AI-native customer and slower demand among established clients.
A broad selloff in technology stocks the prior week sets the background for the upgrade. Observability software from Datadog tracks how applications and cloud infrastructure perform, so more AI tokens moving through customer systems could translate into more activity for the company to monitor and bill.
Second-quarter 2026 results already gave Datadog’s AI story a solid base. The company posted revenue of $1.12 billion, up 35.6% from a year earlier, and non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) of $0.65, beating expectations. That marked Datadog’s fifth consecutive EPS beat.
Datadog’s larger accounts kept expanding as well, with customers paying $100,000 or more in annual recurring revenue up 23% to approximately 4,720. Growth in that tier picked up from 21% in the first quarter of 2026.
Management raised Datadog’s full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $4.45 billion and $4.47 billion after that report. Chief executive Olivier Pomel tied the momentum to AI. He made the point in the August release, stating, “Our customers are building and deploying with AI, and they are using the Datadog platform to observe, secure, and act on their AI-enabled solutions.”
Datadog has been shipping products aimed directly at AI customers, including Bits AI for autonomous incident detection and resolution, AI Guard for protecting AI agents, and Bits Agent Builder for creating custom agents. The company launched more than 100 new capabilities at its DASH 2026 conference, including a Bring Your Own Cloud model that runs Datadog inside customer environments. It also acquired Adaptive ML to speed up its AI research.
That product push came alongside better profitability, with Datadog’s non-GAAP operating margin expanding to 23% from 20% a year earlier. Its free cash flow margin reached 25% in the quarter.
Snowflake and Cloudflare Trail the Leader
Checking in on the peers, Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) stock is up 3%, a solid gain that still trails the jump in Datadog stock. Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is up 0.4% to $297.58, lagging both Datadog stock and Snowflake stock. Snowflake sells a cloud data platform, while Cloudflare runs a network for security and content delivery.
Sector-wide gains are more modest, as the WisdomTree Cloud Computing Fund (NASDAQ:WCLD) is up 0.8%. Broader tech is running ahead of cloud software, as the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is up 1%. That gap leaves the jump in Datadog stock looking like a company-specific reaction to the upgrade.
Bernstein Upgrade Sets Up Datadog’s November Report
Datadog is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 results in early November, with its guidance calling for revenue of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion. Datadog’s report needs to show AI-native customers spending more, since the upgrade rests on AI workload growth. Another focus is whether established customers also step up their spending after the slower demand behind last quarter’s downgrade.
Last quarter’s downgrade is a reminder that Datadog’s growth depends partly on its largest AI-native customer. When all is said and done, investors should keep their Datadog stock positions moderate. A second revenue cut could undo the optimism behind the new rating, and the prior week’s tech selloff showed how quickly sentiment can turn.

Datadog’s (DDOG) Expectations Have Outrun Its Earnings. What Lies Ahead?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 9:42 AM CDT 3 min read
Datadog, Inc. (NASDAQ:DDOG) watches software while it runs. When an application slows or breaks, its tools are what the engineers look at first.
The stock closed at $260.36 on October 19. It has returned 97.7% over the last 6 months, compared with an 11.6% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 8.7% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. The business is growing quickly and earns almost nothing as reported. The share price has behaved as though only the first half of that is true.
READ ALSO: 10 AI Stocks Beyond NVIDIA That Could Surge in 2026
Datadog's (DDOG) Expectations Have Outrun Its Earnings. What Lies Ahead?
What Is Going Right:
Revenue rose 35.60% year on year, and it grows the way good software businesses do, by customers using more rather than buying more. Monitoring scales with how much a customer runs.
The cash is real even where the profit is not. Operating cash flow ran at $1.23 billion against revenue of $3.97 billion, and borrowings are modest enough against equity that a weak year would force nothing.
Datadog is one of the ten in our 10 Most Promising Cloud Stocks According to Hedge Funds. To see the rest of the list, click HERE.
What the Share Price Has Already Counted:
The shares have nearly doubled over six months. Nothing in the reported numbers moved that far, so the move came from what buyers expect rather than from what the company delivered.
The reported margin is the problem with that. Operating profit is 0.67% of revenue, so almost the whole of what the business earns is consumed before it reaches an owner. The gap between that figure and the adjusted one the market quotes is mostly pay issued in shares.
Consumption pricing cuts the other way too. Revenue that rises when customers run more also falls when they run less, and that is not within Datadog's control.
DON'T MISS: 10 Best Stocks to Buy for High Returns in 2026
What Has to Arrive:
The price is 84.75 times what analysts expect next year. That needs the growth to hold and the margin to widen, not one or the other.
Expectations have moved further than earnings over the past six months. The gap closes when earnings catch up or when the price comes back, and the second is quicker.
Monitoring is one slice of a much larger subscription market. 10 Best SaaS Stocks to Buy According to Hedge Funds maps the rest of it.
Conclusion:
The business is doing well, and the share price has done better. Monitoring revenue tracks what a customer consumes, which is a fine way to be paid and explains the growth rate. What has not kept pace is the reported profit, since costs take almost all of it and a large charge for stock issued to staff sits among them. The price now assumes that changes. Watch the margin rather than the revenue, since revenue is the half that is already working.

Datadog, Inc. (NASDAQ:DDOG) was held by 92 hedge funds with a combined stake value of about $3.94 billion at the end of Q2 2026 in the Insider Monkey database. This is up from 80 hedge fund holders in the previous quarter.

Cloud Stocks Retreat as AI Financing Worries Spread: Snowflake and Cloudflare Tumble 7%, Datadog Drops 6%
AI financing fears are dragging high-growth cloud names down far faster than the broader market, and even strong recent earnings cannot seem to stop the bleeding. Here is what separates Snowflake, Cloudflare, and Datadog from each other as investors flee…
Published October 16, 2026, 11:54am ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Cloud software stocks are under heavy pressure as worries about AI financing spread across the sector. High-growth names that posted strong recent results are absorbing much of the selling.
Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW | SNOW Price Prediction) stock is down 7% at $310.83 early in the session, leading the cloud group lower. Likewise, Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is down 7% to $293.45. Meanwhile, Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) stock is down 6% to $249.08, representing a slightly smaller decline than its peers.
Sector funds are falling far less. The First Trust Cloud Computing ETF (NASDAQ:SKYY) is down 4%, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 1.35%. In other words, large-cap tech is slipping but cloud-computing stocks are generally declining faster.
AI Financing Fears Hit High-Growth Cloud Names
This decline extends a rotation out of AI-linked stocks as investors question how AI infrastructure spending gets financed. Snowflake added its own wrinkle in late September, when it proposed a convertible note offering. Those notes can later convert into equity, placing Snowflake directly inside the financing debate.
Each company sells a different piece of the cloud: Snowflake offers a data platform, Cloudflare runs a global network for security and content delivery, and Datadog sells software that tracks applications and infrastructure. That mix ties revenue at all three to cloud usage, so an AI spending pullback could hit them at once (we featured seven suppliers supporting the AI expansion, from power to networking, in a free report you can grab here).
Strong Earnings Haven’t Shielded Snowflake
Snowflake’s latest results were strong. In its Q2 FY2027 report on September 2, Snowflake posted revenue of $1.55 billion, up 35.1% year over year, along with non-GAAP EPS of $0.62 that beat estimates.
Management also raised Snowflake’s fiscal 2027 product revenue guidance to $6.07 billion from $5.84 billion. Its net revenue retention held at 126%, and remaining performance obligations reached $9 billion. Those figures suggest customers are expanding their commitments to the platform.
AI adoption is adding to Snowflake’s momentum. CoCo passed 9,100 accounts in the quarter, while CoWork expanded to 5,800 accounts. Executives called AI a “powerful flywheel” for consumption.
One concern surfaced on Snowflake’s September earnings call. The company cut its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP product gross margin guidance to 74% because fast-growing AI workloads carry a lower contribution margin. Then-CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy stated “As models have gotten more powerful, cost has absolutely become a concern.”
Cloudflare Steers Clear of the AI Capex Race
Cloudflare has taken a more selective path on AI spending, even as it restructures around what it calls an “agentic AI-first operating model.” On its Q2 2026 earnings call in August, then-CEO Matthew Prince explained why Cloudflare avoids selling commodity compute:
I think not all revenue is created equal. And if you’re selling what is just commodity compute, if you’re basically letting, you know, an AI company use your balance sheet and your credit rating in order to buy servers that are the same as everybody else’s servers, that’s just not attractive business for us.
Prince added that Cloudflare has “always focused on how we can squeeze as much out of every CapEx dollar as possible.” That sets Cloudflare apart from hyperscalers that buy servers and lease them back.
Yet, that discipline hasn’t insulated Cloudflare stock. Datadog has leaned into AI with launches such as Bits AI and AI Guard, and Datadog shares are doing slightly better, though still trailing the cloud ETF.
Snowflake’s Financing Question Hangs Over Cloud Names
Snowflake’s bull case rests on demand for data platforms that feed AI workloads, backed by three straight quarters of accelerating product revenue growth. Cloudflare bulls point to its capital discipline, and Datadog bulls to AI monitoring demand. The bear case for all three: investors keep marking down AI-linked names until financing concerns ease.
The next test for Snowflake is whether AI demand keeps product revenue growth on its guided path. Traders may want to check for whether SKYY closes its gap with QQQ.
Strong recent results give Snowflake, Cloudflare, and Datadog a fundamental buffer, while the financing concern could keep the three stocks volatile. Position sizes should be kept small, if you choose to invest at all, until the AI financing question resolves.

Is Most-Watched Stock Datadog, Inc. (DDOG) Worth Betting on Now?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 7:00 AM CDT 5 min read
Datadog (DDOG) has recently been on Zacks.com's list of the most searched stocks. Therefore, you might want to consider some of the key factors that could influence the stock's performance in the near future.
Over the past month, shares of this data analytics and cloud monitoring company have returned +6.3%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's +0.7% change. During this period, the Zacks Internet - Software industry, which Datadog falls in, has gained 2.2%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?
While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.
Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.
Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.
Datadog is expected to post earnings of $0.64 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +16.4%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate remained unchanged.
For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.52 points to a change of +22.9% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has remained unchanged.
For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.96 indicates a change of +17.4% from what Datadog is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.
With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) for Datadog.
The chart below shows the evolution of the company's forward 12-month consensus EPS estimate:
12-month consensus EPS estimate for DDOG
While earnings growth is arguably the most superior indicator of a company's financial health, nothing happens as such if a business isn't able to grow its revenues. After all, it's nearly impossible for a company to increase its earnings for an extended period without increasing its revenues. So, it's important to know a company's potential revenue growth.
For Datadog, the consensus sales estimate for the current quarter of $1.14 billion indicates a year-over-year change of +28.9%. For the current and next fiscal years, $4.46 billion and $5.45 billion estimates indicate +30.2% and +22.2% changes, respectively.
Last Reported Results and Surprise History
Datadog reported revenues of $1.12 billion in the last reported quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +35.6%. EPS of $0.65 for the same period compares with $0.46 a year ago.
Compared to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.08 billion, the reported revenues represent a surprise of +3.85%. The EPS surprise was +12.07%.
The company beat consensus EPS estimates in each of the trailing four quarters. The company topped consensus revenue estimates each time over this period.
No investment decision can be efficient without considering a stock's valuation. Whether a stock's current price rightly reflects the intrinsic value of the underlying business and the company's growth prospects is an essential determinant of its future price performance.
Comparing the current value of a company's valuation multiples, such as its price-to-earnings (P/E), price-to-sales (P/S), and price-to-cash flow (P/CF), to its own historical values helps ascertain whether its stock is fairly valued, overvalued, or undervalued, whereas comparing the company relative to its peers on these parameters gives a good sense of how reasonable its stock price is.
As part of the Zacks Style Scores system, the Zacks Value Style Score (which evaluates both traditional and unconventional valuation metrics) organizes stocks into five groups ranging from A to F (A is better than B; B is better than C; and so on), making it helpful in identifying whether a stock is overvalued, rightly valued, or temporarily undervalued.
Datadog is graded F on this front, indicating that it is trading at a premium to its peers. Click here to see the values of some of the valuation metrics that have driven this grade.
The facts discussed here and much other information on Zacks.com might help determine whether or not it's worthwhile paying attention to the market buzz about Datadog. However, its Zacks Rank #3 does suggest that it may perform in line with the broader market in the near term.

Datadog (DDOG) Stock Is Up, What You Need To Know
What Happened?
Shares of cloud monitoring platform Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) jumped 4.7% in the morning session after easing Treasury yields and broad dip-buying spurred a relief rebound across enterprise software, amplified by Bernstein SocGen Group upgrading the stock to Outperform with a $350 price target.
The relief bid followed a difficult week for cloud providers, with sentiment finding support as the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield retreated to 5.085%, per CNBC reporting, alleviating valuation pressure on high-multiple platforms.
In a note covered by Investing.com, Bernstein raised its price target from $237, citing alternative data indicating enterprise token consumption among major artificial intelligence laboratories grew at least 50% quarter-over-quarter.The rating change reverses Bernstein's prior downgrade, which was prompted by an estimated $100 million annual recurring revenue contract downsizing from Datadog's largest artificial intelligence client and softness across traditional enterprise customers. The broker observed that accelerating generative AI activity is reigniting observability demand, helping offset earlier contract revisions.
When borrowing costs pull back, high-multiple software platforms regain valuation support as future recurring cash flows face lower discount rates. Because heavy model usage requires continuous telemetry to monitor compute costs and query latency, accelerating developer token volumes translate directly into billable software usage, turning concerns over enterprise budget cannibalization into an infrastructure demand hedge.
Is now the time to buy Datadog? Access our full analysis report here, it's free.
Datadog's shares are extremely volatile and have had 38 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.
The previous big move we wrote about was 3 days ago when the stock dropped 7.3% on the news that investors shifted their focus from what AI technology can do toward concerns over how companies will finance it. Driven by these escalating AI funding fears and elevated interest rates, CNBC noted that a massive rotation out of the sector erased more than $1 trillion from the world's largest semiconductor and AI-related stocks this week.
Furthermore, CNBC explained that this funding anxiety triggered counterintuitive moves in the broader market, as investors reassessed the impact of high interest rates on corporate debt-servicing capacity and overall economic growth. Because of these rising structural risks, CNBC reported that safe-haven demand temporarily outweighed inflation fears, prompting capital to exit high-growth tech assets and flow into the Treasury market, which ironically pulled the 10-year Treasury yield down toward 5.09 percent. Ultimately, according to CNBC analysts, this widespread tech sell-off underscores a growing realization on Wall Street that if the capital-intensive AI trade slows due to financing constraints, broader economic growth will likely decelerate as well.
Datadog is up 95.9% since the beginning of the year, but at $262.03 per share, it is still trading 10.7% below its 52-week high of $293.26 from October 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Datadog's shares 5 years ago would now be looking at an investment worth $1,659.

Datadog Reports Q3 on November 4 After Bernstein’s Upgrade. Here’s the Number That Settles the In-House Debate
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 11:26 PM CDT 4 min read
Datadog Reports Q3 on November 4 After Bernstein's Upgrade. Here's the Number That Settles the In-House Debate ©@iJeab via Canva, @kasto via Canva
What Happened?
Datadog (DDOG) closed at $260.36 on October 19, 2026, up 5.36%, after Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform and raised its target to $350 from $237. That target sits above the $340 high in TIKR's October 16 Street data. Shares remain 11.22% below their October 9 closing high of $293.26.
Bernstein's analyst also flagged that customers who get big enough have tended to bring monitoring in-house. Datadog's CFO made a different case a month earlier, and pointed to a runway the upgrade does not address. Third-quarter results arrive before the market opens on November 4, per Datadog's investor relations materials.
Datadog's CFO Says the Cloud Shift Is Still Early
At Goldman Sachs' Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 10, CFO David Obstler pointed to how little of the market has moved. "The research companies say that somewhere upper 20s, 30% of applications are in the cloud," he said. He added that many enterprises "really haven't even started their first material projects." He cited Datadog's customer announcements in banking, insurance, automotive, manufacturing, and airlines as evidence that migration is under way.
To catch those projects, salespeople in Datadog's key accounts group now cover one or two accounts "where the IT budget and conversion to the cloud can be in the tens of millions." On the in-house question, Obstler described AI-native customers moving the other way: "we're seeing a movement from open source or initial efforts or cobbling it together towards Datadog."
Customers with $100,000 or more in annual recurring revenue reached about 4,720 at the end of the second quarter, up 23% from a year earlier. Obstler called these enterprise sales cycles very long, so that count tracks the strategy better than any single quarter's revenue.
Datadog Trades at Twice the Peer Median on Revenue
At the October 16 close, Datadog's enterprise value traded at around 17 times NTM revenue. The median for the nine companies in TIKR's software comparison set, which runs from Microsoft (MSFT) to RingCentral (RNG), was around 8 times. The October 19 gain pushed Datadog's multiple higher.
Margins support part of that premium. Datadog's second-quarter adjusted EBIT margin widened 307 basis points year over year to 22.92%, while revenue grew 35.64%.
The known gap is the largest customer. Datadog said in August that the account had renewed but that its usage would decline starting in the third quarter, a cut built into guidance. Obstler did not claim every customer stays fully on the platform: "it isn't the case all the time, and it also isn't 100% or 0%." Before Bernstein's upgrade, TIKR's October 16 data showed a mean target of around $290, with 33 Buys, 10 Outperforms, 3 Holds, 1 Underperform, and 1 Sell.
The TIKR model's mid case values Datadog at around $726 by December 31, 2030, a total return of around 179% from $260.36, or around 28% a year over 4.2 years. It is a scenario built on assumptions, not a forecast.
Over the model's 2025 to 2035 forecast, the mid case assumes around 21% annual revenue growth and a net income margin near 29%, against 24.4% over the past year on the model card. The primary risk is a valuation reset toward the peer median before those margins arrive.
On the upside, adjusted margins are already widening. On the downside, a multiple at the peer median of around 8 times revenue would be less than half of Datadog's October 16 level.
November 4 shows whether AI-native customers keep moving onto Datadog, as Obstler described, or in-house, as Bernstein warned. Growth in $100,000-plus customers at or above the second quarter's 23% pace would support the premium. A slowdown below 20% would make the gap to the peer median harder to defend.

Is Datadog (DDOG) Priced For More Than Its Cash Flows?
Datadog has delivered a powerful run for shareholders over the past few years, which now puts a spotlight on a simple question for anyone looking at the stock today. Do the company's underlying cash flows support a share price that has moved this far, this fast?
Over the past 3 years, Datadog has returned 203.4%. This raises the stakes on whether its current valuation can still be explained by the cash the business is expected to generate.
Recent product launches that lean on AI capabilities and a broader push into DevSecOps suggest investors are building in expectations for stronger and possibly earlier cash flow. This can meaningfully influence what looks reasonable to pay for the stock today.
If you'd rather focus on sales, this one's for you. See why Datadog's 24.6x P/S tells a different valuation story.
For investors, the debate is whether Datadog's current share price is in line with what its projected cash flows justify when run through a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) lens.
To cross check whether Datadog's recent 203.4% three year return and AI driven story fit your own criteria, it can help to start with a focused list of 35 profitable AI stocks that aren't just burning cash.
Does Datadog Look Undervalued on Cash Flow?
The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model values Datadog by projecting future free cash the business could return to shareholders and then discounting it back to today. On this view, the latest twelve month free cash flow sits at about $1.1b, and the forecast path assumes those cash flows keep growing rather than stalling or shrinking.
The long range projections climb into multiple billions of dollars per year, which means a large portion of the estimated worth comes from what Datadog might earn well into the 2030s rather than from current profits. That kind of growth path leaves the valuation sensitive to changes in assumptions about adoption of newer products, including AI driven tools and the push into DevSecOps. Despite the recent rally and insider selling linked to preset trading plans, the DCF output still places Datadog's estimated intrinsic value modestly above the current share price of $271.34, which suggests that the market has not fully closed that gap yet. Datadog Soars 6% on Bernstein Upgrade as AI Token Use Has “Grown at Least 50%”
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 2:06 PM CDT 3 min read
Datadog Soars 6% on Bernstein Upgrade as AI Token Use Has "Grown at Least 50%" ©@jittawit21 from jittawit21 via Canva, @KanawatTH via Canva
Datadog shares rose 6% today after Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform and raised its price target to $350 from $237.
Bernstein's case for faster AI-driven growth looks well-founded, but the stock already prices in a lot of it.
Analysts expect revenue to grow about 30% this year, then slow to about 23% a year through 2028.
Third-quarter results on Nov. 4 are the first real test of whether AI-native customers can make up for slower traditional customers.
Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) shares are up 6% today. Before the open, Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform from Market Perform and raised its price target to $350 from $237.
The bounce follows a drop of about 14% last week in a broad tech selloff.
It's quite the reversal. Bernstein downgraded Datadog last quarter for two reasons. Its largest "Born in AI" customer (widely reported to be OpenAI) cut about $100 million of annual recurring revenue. And demand looked softer among the traditional customers that make up around 85% of revenue. At the time, Bernstein expected growth from AI-native customers to slow to 50%-60% in 2027, from 80%-90% this year.
Now Bernstein analyst Peter Weed says that view was too conservative:
"Our alt data signals suggest enterprise token consumption appears to have grown at least 50% [quarter over quarter] among the largest AI Labs (and perhaps even faster in their smaller 'Born in AI' customers)."
He added that consumer AI agents like Muse and Dots could raise the monitoring needs of Datadog's traditional customers too.
Wall Street's estimates already have Datadog growing fast for years…
Datadog (DDOG): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023–2028 (TIKR)
Consensus has revenue climbing about 30% this year to $4.47 billion, then slowing to about 23% a year, reaching $6.78 billion in 2028. Bernstein is betting against that slowdown. If the biggest AI labs keep adding usage at anything like 50% a quarter, those later years look conservative to me.
Of course, more tokens don't turn straight into Datadog revenue. And Weed himself points out that customers who get big enough have tended to move monitoring in-house.
Shares were up about 82% this year through Friday's close, and the valuation has followed…
Datadog (DDOG): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)
At Friday's close, Datadog traded at 93.2x forward earnings, and after today's jump it's closer to 99x. That's under its five-year average of 107.6x, which the 2021 bubble pushed up. But it's about double the 47.4x the stock hit in February.
My take: Bernstein's upgrade looks well-founded. If AI-native customers keep growing like this, Datadog's revenue should beat what the Street expects for 2027 and 2028.
But at nearly 100x forward earnings, the stock needs proof. Datadog reports third-quarter results on Nov. 4. That will be the first real look at whether its AI-native customers are making up for any slowdown among its traditional ones.

Datadog Announces Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
Second quarter revenue grew 36% year-over-year to $1.12 billion
Robust growth of larger customers, with about 4,720 $100k+ ARR customers, up from about 3,850 a year ago
Launched AI-powered Bits Code, Bits Chat, and Bits Agent Builder for general availability
NEW YORK-- Datadog, Inc. (NASDAQ:DDOG), the leading AI-powered observability and security platform, today announced financial results for its second quarter ended June 30, 2026.
"Datadog delivered a strong quarter, with 36% year-over-year revenue growth, $316 million in operating cash flow, and $279 million in free cash flow," said Olivier Pomel, co-founder and CEO of Datadog. "Our customers are building and deploying with AI, and they are using the Datadog platform to observe, secure, and act on their AI-enabled solutions."
Pomel added, "We are innovating rapidly to help our customers manage rising complexity, and increasingly build autonomy into their operations."
Second Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights:
•Revenue was $1.12 billion, an increase of 36% year-over-year.
•GAAP operating income was $5 million; GAAP operating margin was 0%.
•Non-GAAP operating income was $257 million; non-GAAP operating margin was 23%.
•GAAP net income per diluted share was $0.12; non-GAAP net income per diluted share was $0.65.
•Operating cash flow was $316 million, with free cash flow of $279 million.
•Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities were $5.0 billion as of June 30, 2026.
Second Quarter & Recent Business Highlights:
•As of June 30, 2026, we had about 4,720 customers with ARR of $100,000 or more, an increase of 23% from about 3,850 as of June 30, 2025.
•Named a Leader in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Observability Platforms, 2026. This is the sixth consecutive year Gartner has positioned Datadog as a Leader in the Magic Quadrant.
•Acquired Adaptive ML, a frontier AI startup developing the world’s first Reinforcement Learning Operations platform, to accelerate Datadog AI Research’s investment in world models and agentic LLM post-training for observability—combining Datadog’s access to real-world infrastructure and security data with Adaptive ML’s expertise in building specialized, high-performance AI agents.
•Launched more than 100 new capabilities at DASH 2026 to help customers drive autonomy and manage growing AI and security complexity. Highlights included fully autonomous Bits AI for end-to-end incident detection, investigation, and remediation; AI Guard to protect AI agents from prompt injection and poisoning attacks; Bring Your Own Cloud for deploying Datadog within customer environments; and Bits Agent Builder for creating custom AI agents.
Third Quarter and Full Year 2026 Outlook:
Based on information as of today, August 6, 2026, Datadog is providing the following guidance:
•Third Quarter 2026 Outlook:
◦Revenue between $1.135 billion and $1.145 billion.
◦Non-GAAP operating income between $260 million and $270 million.
◦Non-GAAP net income per share between $0.63 and $0.65, assuming approximately 378 million weighted average diluted shares outstanding.
•Full Year 2026 Outlook:
◦Revenue between $4.45 billion and $4.47 billion.
◦Non-GAAP operating income between $1.01 billion and $1.03 billion.
◦Non-GAAP net income per share between $2.50 and $2.54, assuming approximately 376 million weighted average diluted shares outstanding.
Datadog has not reconciled its expectations as to non-GAAP operating income, or as to non-GAAP net income per share, to their most directly comparable GAAP measure as a result of uncertainty regarding, and the potential variability of, reconciling items such as stock-based compensation and employer payroll taxes on equity incentive plans. Accordingly, reconciliation is not available without unreasonable effort, although it is important to note that these factors could be material to Datadog’s results computed in accordance with GAAP.
Conference Call Details:
•What: Datadog financial results for the second quarter of 2026 and outlook for the third quarter and the full year 2026
•When: August 6, 2026 at 8:00 A.M. Eastern Time (5:00 A.M. Pacific Time)
•Dial in: To access the call in the U.S., please register here. Callers are encouraged to dial into the call 10 to 15 minutes prior to the start to prevent any delay in joining.
•Webcast: https://investors.datadoghq.com (live and replay)
•Replay: A replay of the call will be archived on the investor relations website
Datadog is the leading observability and security platform for the AI era, providing businesses with unified visibility across the technology stack to manage complexity at scale. It brings applications, infrastructure, data, models, and security into one place, using AI to detect and resolve issues before they impact customers. Trusted globally by Fortune 500 companies and high-growth AI leaders, Datadog enables businesses to move faster with clarity and confidence.
This press release and the earnings call referencing this press release contain “forward-looking” statements, as that term is defined under the federal securities laws, including but not limited to statements regarding Datadog’s strategy, product and platform capabilities, the growth in and ability to capitalize on long-term market opportunities including the pace and scope of cloud migration, digital transformation and AI deployment, gross margins, operating margins including with respect to sales and marketing, research and development expenses, net interest and other income, cash taxes, capital expenditures and capitalized software, and Datadog’s future financial performance, including its outlook for the third quarter and the full year 2026third quarter and the full year 2026 and related notes and assumptions. These forward-looking statements are based on Datadog’s current assumptions, expectations and beliefs and are subject to substantial risks, uncertainties, assumptions and changes in circumstances that may cause Datadog’s actual results, performance or achievements to differ materially from those expressed or implied in any forward-looking statement.
The risks and uncertainties referred to above include, but are not limited to (1) our recent rapid growth may not be indicative of our future growth; (2) our history of operating losses; (3) our limited operating history; (4) our dependence on existing customers purchasing additional subscriptions and products from us and renewing their subscriptions; (5) our ability to attract new customers; (6) our ability to effectively develop and expand our sales and marketing capabilities; (7) risk of a security breach; (8) risk of interruptions or performance problems associated with our products and platform capabilities; (9) our ability to adapt and respond to rapidly changing technology or customer needs; (10) the competitive markets in which we participate; (11) risks associated with successfully managing our growth; (12) risks associated with changing laws, regulations, and contractual obligations related to data privacy and security and (13) general market, political, economic, and business conditions including concerns about trade policies, tariffs, reduced economic growth and associated decreases in information technology spending. These risks and uncertainties are more fully described in our filings with
the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), including in the section entitled “Risk Factors” in our Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, filed with the SEC on February 18, 2026. Additional information will be made available in our Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 and other filings and reports that we may file from time to time with the SEC. Moreover, we operate in a very competitive and rapidly changing environment. New risks emerge from time to time. It is not possible for our management to predict all risks, nor can we assess the impact of all factors on our business or the extent to which any factor, or combination of factors, may cause actual results to differ materially from those contained in any forward-looking statements we may make. In light of these risks, uncertainties and assumptions, we cannot guarantee future results, levels of activity, performance, achievements, or events and circumstances reflected in the forward-looking statements will occur. Forward-looking statements represent our beliefs and assumptions only as of the date of this press release. We disclaim any obligation to update forward-looking statements.
Datadog discloses the following non-GAAP financial measures in this release and the earnings call referencing this press release: non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP gross margin, non-GAAP operating expenses (research and development, sales and marketing and general and administrative), non-GAAP operating income (loss), non-GAAP operating margin, non-GAAP net income (loss), non-GAAP net income (loss) per diluted share, non-GAAP net income (loss) per basic share, free cash flow and free cash flow margin. Datadog uses each of these non-GAAP financial measures internally to understand and compare operating results across accounting periods, for internal budgeting and forecasting purposes, for short- and long-term operating plans, and to evaluate Datadog’s financial performance. Datadog believes they are useful to investors, as a supplement to GAAP measures, in evaluating its operational performance, as further discussed below. Datadog’s non-GAAP financial measures may not provide information that is directly comparable to that provided by other companies in its industry, as other companies in its industry may calculate non-GAAP financial results differently, particularly related to non-recurring and unusual items. In addition, there are limitations in using non-GAAP financial measures because the non-GAAP financial measures are not prepared in accordance with GAAP and may be different from non-GAAP financial measures used by other companies and exclude expenses that may have a material impact on Datadog’s reported financial results.
Non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered in isolation from, or as a substitute for, financial information prepared in accordance with GAAP. A reconciliation of the historical non-GAAP financial measures to their most directly comparable GAAP measures has been provided in the financial statement tables included below in this press release.
Datadog defines non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP gross margin, non-GAAP operating expenses (research and development, sales and marketing and general and administrative), non-GAAP operating income (loss), non-GAAP operating margin and non-GAAP net income (loss) as the respective GAAP balances, adjusted for,
as applicable: (1) stock-based compensation expense; (2) the amortization of acquired intangibles; (3) employer payroll taxes on employee stock transactions; (4) M&A transaction costs; (5) amortization of issuance costs; and (6) an assumed provision for income taxes based on our long-term projected tax rate. Non-GAAP financial measures prior to April 1, 2025 have not been adjusted for M&A transaction costs, as such costs were not material to our results of operations in such prior periods. Our estimated long-term projected tax rate is subject to change for a variety of reasons, including the rapidly evolving global tax environment, significant changes in Datadog's geographic earnings mix, or other changes to our strategy or business operations. We will re-evaluate our long-term projected tax rate as appropriate. Datadog defines free cash flow as net cash provided by operating activities, minus capital expenditures and minus capitalized software development costs, if any. Investors are encouraged to review the reconciliation of these historical non-GAAP financial measures to their most directly comparable GAAP financial measures.
Management believes these non-GAAP financial measures are useful to investors and others in assessing Datadog’s operating performance due to the following factors:
Stock-based compensation. Datadog utilizes stock-based compensation to attract and retain employees. It is principally aimed at aligning their interests with those of its stockholders and at long-term retention, rather than to address operational performance for any particular period. As a result, stock-based compensation expenses vary for reasons that are generally unrelated to financial and operational performance in any particular period.
Amortization of acquired intangibles. Datadog views amortization of acquired intangible assets as items arising from pre-acquisition activities determined at the time of an acquisition. While these intangible assets are evaluated for impairment regularly, amortization of the cost of acquired intangibles is an expense that is not typically affected by operations during any particular period.
Employer payroll taxes on employee stock transactions. Datadog excludes employer payroll tax expense on equity incentive plans as these expenses are tied to the exercise or vesting of underlying equity awards and the price of Datadog’s common stock at the time of vesting or exercise. As a result, these taxes may vary in any particular period independent of the financial and operating performance of Datadog’s business.
M&A transaction costs. Datadog views acquisition-related expenses, such as transaction costs, as costs that are not necessarily reflective of operational performance during a period. In particular, Datadog believes the consideration of measures that exclude such expenses can assist in the comparison of operational performance in different periods which may or may not include such expenses.
Amortization of issuance costs. In June 2020 and December 2024, Datadog issued $747.5 million of 0.125% convertible senior notes due 2025 and $1.0 billion of 0% convertible senior notes due 2029, respectively. Debt issuance costs, which reduce the carrying value of the convertible debt instrument, are amortized as interest expense over the term. The expense for the amortization of debt issuance costs is a non-cash item, and we believe the exclusion of this interest expense will provide for a more useful comparison of our operational performance in different periods.
Additionally, Datadog’s management believes that the non-GAAP financial measure free cash flow is meaningful to investors because it is a measure of liquidity that provides useful information in understanding and evaluating the strength of our liquidity and future ability to generate cash that can be used for strategic opportunities or investing in our business. Free cash flow represents net cash provided by operating activities, reduced by capital expenditures and capitalized software development costs, if any. The reduction of capital expenditures and amounts capitalized for software development facilitates comparisons of Datadog's liquidity on a period-to-period basis and excludes items that management does not consider to be indicative of our liquidity.
Datadog’s number of customers with ARR of $100,000 or more is based on the ARR of each customer, as of the last month of the quarter.
We define the number of customers as the number of accounts with a unique account identifier for which we have an active subscription in the period indicated. Users of our free trials or tier are not included in our customer count. A single organization with multiple divisions, segments or subsidiaries is generally counted as a single customer. However, in some cases where they have separate billing terms, we may count separate divisions, segments or subsidiaries as multiple customers.

Amphenol designs, manufactures and markets electrical, electronic and fiber optic connectors, interconnect systems, antennas, sensors and sensor-based products, and coaxial, high-speed, fiber optic and specialty cable. The company is headquartered in Wallingford, Connecticut.
Amphenol's manufacturing facilities are generally vertically integrated operations, from initial design through final manufacturing. The company designs, manufactures and assembles products at facilities in approximately 40 countries. It sells products through its global sales force, independent representatives and a network of electronics distributors. Customers range from OEMs to contract manufacturers in its served end markets.
Amphenol reported net sales of $23.1 billion in 2025. The company's products are typically designed into customer systems and platforms. Effective Jan 1, 2022, the company aligned its businesses into three reportable segments: (i) Harsh Environment Solutions, (ii) Communications Solutions and (iii) Interconnect and Sensor Systems.
Harsh Environment Solutions designs, manufactures and markets ruggedized interconnect products. Offerings include connectors and interconnect systems, printed circuits and printed circuit assemblies and related products used in demanding environments.
Communications Solutions designs, manufactures and markets connector and interconnect systems. Products include high speed, radio frequency, power and fiber optic interconnect offerings, together with antennas, that are used across data, broadband and wireless infrastructure.
Interconnect and Sensor Systems designs, manufactures and markets sensors and sensor-based systems, connectors and value-add interconnect systems.
Automotive, broadband communications, commercial aerospace, communications networks, defense, industrial, information technology and data communications and mobile devices are primary end markets served by the company.
